title: A History of Rebellion
sum: Elders of the exile come to Ezekiel's house to ask the LORD for a word, on a day in August 591 BC (20:1). The LORD refuses to be asked (20:3) and tells Ezekiel to put them on trial by telling their own history (20:4). The story has three rounds: Egypt (20:5–9), the wilderness (20:10–26) and the land (20:27–31). Each time Israel rebels, the LORD thinks of pouring out his rage, and each time he holds back "for the sake of my name", so that the nations will not see his name profaned.

Then the chapter turns. The elders want to be like the nations (20:32), but the LORD will rule over them, bring them out and into a new wilderness, and sort them there (20:33–38). The faithful will worship on his holy mountain and be ashamed of what they did (20:40–44). The last five verses (English 20:45–49, Hebrew 21:1–5) are a short oracle of a fire in the southern forest, and the prophet's complaint that people say he only tells parables.
readings: Read as history

Ezekiel gives a survey of Israel's past, with details that Exodus and Numbers do not give: idols in Egypt (20:7–8), a second rebellion by the children in the wilderness (20:21), the oath to scatter (20:23). Some readers think he used traditions we have lost. On this reading, 20:1–44 tells the elders something true about their ancestors that they would rather not hear.
Read as preaching

Ezekiel retells the story the way a preacher shapes it, as Psalm 78, Psalm 106 and Nehemiah 9 do. The past is bent to the point: rebellion is as old as the nation, and the LORD's mercy has never been earned. Chapters 16 and 23 do the same with other images. On this reading the details are less important than the argument.
Read with 20:25–26 at the center

Some readers take the "rules that were not good" as the heart of the chapter, since it is where the LORD's own part in Israel's ruin is stated plainly. The "good" rules of 20:11 are matched by the "not good" rules of 20:25, and the chapter becomes a study in how rejecting life-giving law leads to law that does not give life.

views.H: The seventh year (591 BC) falls between the Temple vision of 8:1 (592) and the siege-day of 24:1 (588). The elders probably wanted to know how long the exile would last. Ezekiel gives no date; he gives a history and a promise: the LORD will bring them out and gather them. The return under Cyrus (539 BC) is the nearest historical fulfillment, though only some returned.
views.C: The chapter is one of the best-studied in the book. Zimmerli's commentary finds later expansion in places (for example in 20:27–29); Greenberg and Block read it as a unity. All agree that Ezekiel's account of Israel's origins, with rebellion beginning in Egypt, differs sharply from Exodus, and that it is not a historical record in the strict sense but a theological retelling.
views.J: Rashi reads the "rules that were not good" as the LORD delivering Israel into the hands of their temptation, and he notes that Targum Jonathan renders the verse as the people following their foolish inclination and making decrees that were not good (Sefaria). In the Sephardi custom Ezekiel 20:2–20 is the haftarah for Kedoshim (Leviticus 19–20), and Ezekiel 22:1–16 is the Sephardi haftarah for Acharei Mot (Leviticus 16–18); Ashkenazi lists differ, and several give Amos 9:7–15 for these portions (reported by the Wikipedia table of haftarot, which notes that printed editions disagree). The Sabbath emphasis of the chapter fits the Jewish place of Sabbath as the sign of the covenant.
views.X: Christian readers have linked 20:11 ("by which a human being who does them will live") with Leviticus 18:5, which Paul quotes in Romans 10:5 and Galatians 3:12, and have disagreed about what Paul means. The wilderness oath of 20:15 appears in Hebrews 3–4. Luke 23:31 may echo the green and dry tree of 20:47. The rules "not good" of 20:25 can be read as law given in judgment, as the people's own decrees, as the customs of the nations or as the firstborn law taken literally; readers who hold with Paul that the commandment is "holy and good" (Romans 7:12) do not read it as a charge against the Torah.
views.F: Some futurist readers (premillennial and others) take the gathering from the nations and the trial in the wilderness of the peoples (20:34–38) as a still-future regathering of Israel before the end. Others see it fulfilled in the return from Babylon or in the church. Jewish readers have linked the passage with the gathering of exiles in the messianic age.

deep.h: Which witnesses were read for this part
deep.b: For chapters 20 to 24 the Hebrew was read word by word from the Leningrad Codex. The Dead Sea Scrolls were checked with the Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcription (ETCBC dss): no Ezekiel scroll preserves chapters 20, 21 or 22; 4QEzek-a (4Q73) preserves parts of 23:14, 15, 17 and 18 (not 23:16) and of 23:44–47; 4QEzek-c (4Q75) preserves parts of 24:2–3. The Greek was read in Swete's edition, which prints Codex Vaticanus. Papyrus 967 (which preserves Ezekiel from chapter 11 on) and the apparatus of Ziegler's Göttingen edition were not read for this part, so wherever this part says "the Greek" it means Codex Vaticanus as Swete prints it. Rashi on 20:25, 21:8, 21:32 and 23:4, Radak on 21:32 and 23:4, the Targum on 20:25 and 21:32, and Bavli Shabbat 55a were read in the English on Sefaria. The numbering is the English one; Hebrew 21:1–5 is English 20:45–49 and Hebrew 21:6–37 is English 21:1–32.

Each round has the same shape. The LORD acts for Israel and gives a command (Egypt: throw away your idols, 20:7; wilderness: keep my rules and Sabbaths, 20:11–12, 18–20; the land: no command is needed, since the land was the gift). Israel rebels (20:8, 13, 21, 28). The LORD thinks of rage (20:8, 13, 21). He acts "for the sake of my name" (20:9, 14, 22). Then comes an oath of the raised hand (20:15, 23). The last round breaks the pattern, since there the LORD does not hold back: the shrines on the hills (20:28–29) lead to the present, and the present generation is the one before him (20:30–31). The sequence is the same as the speeches of Psalm 78 and Psalm 106, but those psalms end with mercy and Ezekiel ends with a trial.

The reason the LORD gives for saving Israel is not their goodness but his reputation among the nations. If the nations saw his people destroyed, they would think he could not keep them (20:9, 14, 22). The same logic returns in 36:20–23, where the exiles' scattering has already profaned the name, and the LORD acts to restore it. Isaiah 48:9–11 has a similar line, in which the LORD acts for his own sake. Some readers find this theology cold; others find it the strongest ground for hope, since a gift that depends on God's name cannot be lost by the people's failure.

echoes: Exodus 6:6–8; Leviticus 18:5; Numbers 14:21–35; Psalm 78:1–72; Psalm 106:1–48; Nehemiah 9:6–37; Jeremiah 7:21–26; Ezekiel 16:1–63; Ezekiel 36:16–38; Romans 10:5; Galatians 3:12; Hebrews 3:7–19; Luke 23:31

settings.what: The elders' question and the LORD's history lesson
settings.to: Elders of the Judean exile who came to Ezekiel's house in Babylon and sat down in front of him
settings.when: The tenth day of the fifth month of the seventh year of Jehoiachin's exile (about August 591 BC), a year after the Temple vision of chapter 8
settings.why: The elders came for a word, probably about how long the exile would last and whether they could blend in where they lived. The LORD refuses the question and answers with a charge: they are the latest in a long line of rebels. The history is not to shame them for its own sake but to show why he acts as he does (for his name) and to say that he will bring them back, not as they are, but through a trial.
settings.readers: The exiles who read the collected book heard it after Jerusalem had fallen. The long account of rebellion explained how the disaster could have happened, and the promise of 20:40–44 spoke to those still waiting.
views: The text does not state the question. Many read the visit as a request for an oracle about the end of the exile. The saying of 20:32 ("We will be like the nations") shows that some of the exiles were thinking of blending in with Babylon, which may be why the LORD answers as he does.

Most take the "you" as the elders and the whole exile community. Some hold that the child sacrifice charge describes the Judah that was still in the land, as in 20:28–29, and is spoken about them in their absence.

settings.what: The fire in the southern forest
settings.to: Ezekiel, told to face south; the exiles who hear him (the forest is Judah, which lay south-west of Babylon by the road)
settings.when: The same day, or soon after, as 20:1 (no new date is given)
settings.why: A short, vivid warning in the form the elders had complained about: a parable. The forest of the Negev is burned and none can put out the fire. The next chapter explains the picture in plain words (the sword, 21:3–5). Ezekiel's own complaint (20:49) shows that some of his hearers took his words as riddles and ignored them.
settings.readers: The later readers who knew the outcome heard the fire as the burning of the city and the Temple in 586 BC.

title: The Sword Drawn
sum: One sword runs through four oracles. First Ezekiel is told to face Jerusalem and say that the LORD has drawn his sword from its sheath, to cut off the righteous and the wicked alike (21:1–5). He is to groan in front of the elders, so that when they ask why, he can tell them about the news that is coming (21:6–7). Then comes a poem, the song of the sword, sharpened, polished and handed to the one who kills (21:8–17).

Next Ezekiel marks out two roads on the ground where the king of Babylon stands and asks his omens whether to attack Ammon or Jerusalem (21:18–23). The verdict falls on the "profane and wicked leader of Israel", and on the crown and the turban (21:24–27). The last oracle turns the sword on Ammon (21:28–32). The chapter is numbered 21:6–37 in the Hebrew Bible. This site uses the English numbers.
readings: Read as the campaign of 588–586 BC

The sword is Nebuchadnezzar's army. The two roads are the real choice he faced when Judah and Ammon were both in revolt, and the fork in the road is the actual moment when Jerusalem became the target. The "leader" is Zedekiah, whose throne is lost.
Read as a poem of the LORD's sword

The sword belongs to the LORD, and Babylon is its hand. The song (21:9–17) is a war poem with its own logic, which uses the old imagery of the LORD's sharpened sword and flashing lightning. On this reading the historical details are the occasion, not the content.
Read as a messianic promise

The line "until he comes whose right it is" (21:27) points beyond Zedekiah to a ruler to come, in the tradition of Genesis 49:10. Christian commentators have read this as a prophecy of Christ. Rashi, Radak and the Targum read it of a historical figure (see the note), and none of them takes it of the Messiah.

views.H: Nebuchadnezzar's campaign reached Judah after Zedekiah's revolt, probably in 589 or 588 BC. Jeremiah 27 shows Ammon and others in Jerusalem plotting revolt; 40:14 shows Ammon's king later working against Gedaliah. Ezekiel's "two roads" are a way of saying that the LORD, not an omen, directed the choice. Ammon, too, fell to Babylon within some years.
views.C: Critics see the chapter as a collection. The sword song (21:9–17) may be an older poem. Some critical scholars suggest additions in 21:23–24. Greenberg reads the chapter as a planned whole. The Hebrew text of the song (21:10, 13, 15) is among the hardest in the book, with rare words and possible corruption.
views.J: Rashi (on Hebrew 21:8) reads "the righteous and the wicked" as "the moist and the dry", the green and dry trees of 20:47. Rashi on 21:27 reads the ruin as the kingdom passing from Jeconiah to Zedekiah to Gedaliah and not lasting until Ishmael son of Nethaniah, who killed Gedaliah; the Targum of Ezekiel also names Ishmael son of Nethaniah; Radak names Nebuchadnezzar as the one given the judgment. The Talmud's best-known discussion of the righteous who die with the wicked (Bavli Shabbat 55a–b) is built on Ezekiel 9:4–6, the mark on the foreheads, and not on this chapter, but it asks the question that 21:3–4 raises.
views.X: Christian readers have linked 21:27 with Genesis 49:10 ("until Shiloh comes") and read it of Christ, the one whose right it is to rule. The sword also appears in the New Testament as the sword of the Word (Hebrews 4:12; Revelation 19:15). The green and dry trees of the previous oracle (20:47) may be echoed in Luke 23:31.
views.F: Some futurist readers take the Messiah of 21:27 as one yet to come in power. Others, noting that Ezekiel's own context is Zedekiah's fall, see the verse as met in Christ's first coming or in the judgments of 586 BC.

deep.b: The oracle gives a pagan king three methods of finding the will of his gods: arrows, household idols and a liver. All three were used in Mesopotamia and are known from texts and from clay models of livers. Ezekiel's point is not to endorse them. The omen "points" to Jerusalem (21:22), but the real author of the choice is the LORD, who uses the king's own religion to steer his army. This is the same idea as Isaiah 10:5–15 (Assyria as the rod of God's anger) and Jeremiah 27:6 (Nebuchadnezzar as the LORD's servant). It also means that Jerusalem's people, who thought the omen false (21:23), were wrong for the wrong reason: they trusted their oaths and not the LORD.

deep.h: Poetry and prose in this chapter
deep.b: Chapter 21 changes form. The groaning sign and the roads are prose. The song of the sword (21:9–17) is poetry in short lines. The oracle on Ammon (21:28–32) returns to the poem's rhythm in its first verses. This Plain sets the poems in lines, separated by slashes. The verse breaks are the English ones.

echoes: Genesis 49:10; Deuteronomy 32:41–42; Jeremiah 27:1–11; Jeremiah 47:6–7; Isaiah 10:5–15; Ezekiel 25:1–7; Luke 23:31; Revelation 19:15

settings.what: The LORD's sword and the prophet's groan
settings.by: The LORD, through Ezekiel, who is to act out the message
settings.to: The exiles who watch Ezekiel (the oracle is addressed to Jerusalem and the land of Israel)
settings.when: No date; the chapter follows 20:1 (591 BC) and comes before 24:1 (588 BC)
settings.why: Ezekiel is to groan in front of the exiles so that they ask why. His answer prepares them for news of Jerusalem's fall. The sign shows them what the news will do to them, before it comes. The point is that no one, including the righteous, will be left outside the sword's path.
settings.readers: Exiles who read this after 586 knew the news; the sign was fulfilled when the survivor came (33:21).

settings.to: Jerusalem and the leaders of Israel, spoken in Babylon to the exiles
settings.when: No date; before the siege of 588 BC
settings.why: A war poem that makes the sword real to those who hear. It calls on Ezekiel to wail and slap his thigh, and the LORD claps his hands at the end. The poem shows that the coming disaster is the LORD's act and not an accident of politics.
settings.readers: Later readers saw the sword fall in 586; the poem became a record of why.

settings.by: The LORD, through Ezekiel's sign act
settings.to: The exiles, who watch Ezekiel draw the roads; the oracle addresses Jerusalem's "leader"
settings.when: No date; most likely 589 or 588 BC, as Judah and Ammon were in revolt against Babylon
settings.why: To tell the exiles that the Babylonian army's march is not chance. The omens of a pagan king serve the LORD's purpose, and Jerusalem, which thought it was safe, will be taken. The verses about the leader tell Zedekiah that his crown will be removed.
settings.readers: The exiles who knew that Zedekiah had been blinded and his sons killed (2 Kings 25:7) heard the verdict fulfilled.
views: Most take the "profane and wicked leader" as Zedekiah. Others take it as the line of Judah's kings in general.
Who is the one "whose right it is"

Rashi: the one God charged to carry out his vengeance, with the kingdom passing to Gedaliah and then to Ishmael son of Nethaniah. Targum: Ishmael son of Nethaniah. Radak: Nebuchadnezzar. Christian commentators: Christ, with Genesis 49:10. Other commentators: the rightful Davidic ruler promised in 34:23–24 and 37:24.

settings.to: The Ammonites, spoken about in front of the exiles; also a warning to Judah, which had plotted with Ammon
settings.when: No date; probably shortly after the oracle of 21:18–27
settings.why: Ammon had taunted Judah and would not escape. The oracle shows that the sword goes beyond Jerusalem. Ammon will meet its end in its own land, and its name will be forgotten.
settings.readers: After 586 readers saw it as the other side of Jerusalem's fall; the Ammon oracle of 25:1–7 gives the reason in full.

title: The City of Bloodshed
sum: Ezekiel is told to put Jerusalem on trial. The charges come in a long list: murder, idols, contempt for parents, oppression of the foreigner and the orphan and the widow, despising the holy things and the Sabbaths, slander, incest, bribes and interest (22:1–12). The LORD strikes his hands together at the blood and the unjust gain, and promises to scatter the city's people and to burn the uncleanness out of them (22:13–16).

A second oracle turns the house of Israel into dross: all copper, tin, iron and lead, and no silver, to be gathered into Jerusalem as into a furnace and melted (22:17–22). A third indicts every class: prophets, priests, officials and the people of the land (22:23–29). Its last verse, 22:30, is among the best known in the book: the LORD looked for someone to stand in the gap, and found no one.
readings: Read as a legal indictment

The chapter reads like a prosecutor's case. The list of crimes follows the Holiness Code of Leviticus 17–26, and the verdict is a sentence. On this reading Ezekiel is a prophet-judge who shows the city that it has broken the covenant it knows.
Read as the picture of a society

The three oracles show a city whose every class has failed: the court, the Temple, the market, the palace and the landowners. The point is the whole fabric, not a list of sins. Zephaniah 3:3–4 draws a similar picture.
Read through 22:30

The final verse is read as a statement about intercession: the LORD wanted someone to plead for the land, and there was none. Others read it as the final proof that the judgment was just. See the note.

views.H: The chapter belongs to the years before the siege (about 591 to 588 BC), when Jerusalem was crowded and the leaders were making promises to Egypt. Its charges of bribes, interest and oppression fit what Jeremiah says of the same years (Jeremiah 5; 7; 22). The furnace of 22:17–22 describes the siege, when refugees filled the city.
views.C: The chapter is often taken as composite. 22:1–16 and 22:23–31 are indictments, and 22:17–22 is a separate image. The links with the Holiness Code (Leviticus 17–26) are a major topic: Milgrom thinks Ezekiel knew the Code; Kohn argues the influence runs the other way. The Greek differs in 22:25 and 22:30, where it may preserve an earlier or a simpler text.
views.J: In the Sephardi custom Ezekiel 22:1–16 is the haftarah for Acharei Mot (Leviticus 16–18); Ashkenazi lists differ, and the Vilna Gaon and others are reported to prefer Amos 9:7–15 because Ezekiel 22 speaks harshly of Jerusalem (reported by the Wikipedia table of haftarot). The charge that the priests do not tell the holy from the common (22:26) repeats Leviticus 10:10–11, which is read in the Torah cycle.
views.X: Christian readers have used 22:30 in teaching on intercession and have seen Christ as the one who stands in the gap (compare Hebrews 7:25). The furnace image has been linked to the refining of the church (1 Peter 1:7), though in Ezekiel the furnace destroys.
views.F: Few futurist readings centre on this chapter, which is tied to the siege of 588 to 586 BC.

deep.b: Almost every item in 22:7–12 has a counterpart in the laws of Leviticus 17–26. Contempt for parents (Leviticus 19:3; 20:9), oppression of the foreigner (19:33–34), the Sabbaths (19:30), slander (19:16), incest and adultery (chapters 18 and 20), bribes (19:15) and interest (25:36–37). Some conclude that Ezekiel knew a written Holiness Code and quotes it by allusion. Others hold that the Code was shaped partly by Ezekiel's circle, or that both draw on a common body of priestly teaching. The question has no agreed answer, and the Plain does not rest on one.

A refiner melts silver ore to separate the metal from the waste. In Isaiah 1:25 the LORD promises to smelt away the dross so that something pure remains. In Jeremiah 6:27–30 the refiner works in vain, because the waste cannot be separated. Ezekiel goes further than Jeremiah: the house of Israel is all waste, and the furnace is lit only to melt it. The reader who knows Zechariah 13:9 and Malachi 3:2–3 knows that the furnace later becomes a means of purification. In Ezekiel the purifying comes only after the melting, in the new heart of 36:26.

echoes: Leviticus 17–26; Isaiah 1:22–25; Jeremiah 5:1; Jeremiah 6:27–30; Zephaniah 3:3–4; Psalm 106:23; Ezekiel 13:5; Ezekiel 14:14; Ezekiel 24:6–14

settings.what: The trial of the city of bloodshed
settings.by: The LORD, through Ezekiel as prosecutor
settings.to: Jerusalem, spoken in Babylon to the exiles who knew the city
settings.when: No date; before the siege, most likely 591 to 589 BC
settings.why: To name the city's sins, one by one, so that the coming judgment is seen to be earned. The list reaches every part of life: family, worship, court, market, bed. The final threat of scattering tells the exiles that more people will join them.
settings.readers: The exiles and later readers needed the list to see that the fall of the city was no accident or injustice.

settings.what: The house of Israel as dross
settings.to: The house of Israel; the oracle speaks of those who will be gathered to Jerusalem
settings.when: No date; before or during the early siege
settings.why: To say that the siege will not purify: the people who gather in the city are waste, and the furnace will melt them. It prepares the exiles for the idea that the people of Jerusalem have no merit.
settings.readers: After the fall, the image explained why the survivors needed more than a refining: a new heart (36:26).

settings.to: The land of Israel, spoken to the exiles; the accused are prophets, priests, officials and the people of the land
settings.when: No date; before the fall of the city
settings.why: To show that no group could have saved the city. The priests did not teach, the prophets lied, the officials preyed, the landowners cheated. The last verse says that even one honest voice could have turned the judgment, and there was none.
settings.readers: The exiles who had been among these classes needed to hear that the LORD had looked for help before he sent judgment.
views: Some read the verse as a call for intercession; others as the final proof that no one could be found. See the note on the gap.

title: Oholah and Oholibah
sum: The story of two sisters, daughters of one mother, who both prostitute themselves in Egypt in their youth and then become the LORD's wives (23:1–4). The older, Oholah (Samaria), lusts for the Assyrians and is given to them to be killed (23:5–10). The younger, Oholibah (Jerusalem), sees this and does worse. She falls in love with painted pictures of Chaldean officers, sends for them, is used and thrown aside, and turns back to Egypt (23:11–21).

The LORD will rouse her lovers against her (23:22–35). They will mutilate her and take her children, and she will drink her sister's cup of horror. The last part joins both sisters in one charge: adultery, child sacrifice and the defiling of the sanctuary on the same day (23:36–49). The sentence is stoning and burning, so that every woman will be warned.
readings: Read as an allegory of alliances

The two sisters are the two kingdoms, and the lovers are the great powers. The charge is about politics: Samaria and Jerusalem trusted Assyria, Egypt and Babylon rather than the LORD. On this reading the sexual language is the prophets' usual picture of political and religious faithlessness.
Read as a text that harms

Critics argue that the chapter makes a woman's body and its punishment a picture of sin, and that its violence can teach readers to see abuse as holy. On this reading the allegory must be read with care and sometimes against its own grain.
Read as shock therapy

Defenders argue that the language is meant to horrify the exiles, who thought themselves innocent, and that the real target is the people's behavior. The shock is the point. The same people who hear it are the "wife" the LORD speaks to.

views.H: Samaria fell in 722/721 BC to Assyria (2 Kings 17); Jerusalem's lovers were Assyria (Ahaz), Egypt and Babylon (Hezekiah, Zedekiah). The Chaldean wall pictures and the sending of messengers (23:14–16) fit Hezekiah's embassy and Judah's later diplomacy. The punishment of 23:22–35 is the siege of 588–586 BC.
views.C: Chapter 23 is paired with chapter 16 and shares a pattern with Hosea 1–3 and Jeremiah 3:6–11. Many critics see an older core extended in the exile; 23:36–49 is often seen as a later addition because it changes the voice and adds child sacrifice and Temple defilement. The Greek differs at several points (23:20, 34, 42, 43).
views.J: Rashi and Radak on 23:4 (read on Sefaria) identify Oholah with Samaria and Oholibah with Jerusalem. Rashi takes the names as nicknames: Samaria is a "tent" because from the start it was tied to Jeroboam's calves and Ahab's Baal temple, and Jerusalem is the city where God's tent and sanctuary stood. Radak reads "her tent is not mine" and "my tent is in her" the same way. The cup of 23:32 joins the cup-of-wrath tradition of Jeremiah 25.
views.X: Christian readers have read the sisters as an image of unfaithful Israel, with the church as the bride in the Song of Songs and Revelation. The cup passage lies behind Gethsemane and the cups of wrath in Revelation. Few churches read the chapter aloud; modern readers, Christian and Jewish, raise the questions of the second reading.
views.F: Futurist readers have used the chapter little, apart from comparisons with the harlot of Revelation 17, a link the text itself does not make.

deep.h: How to read the chapter today
deep.b:
Ezekiel 23 and its twin, chapter 16, are the two hardest chapters of the book to read aloud. They describe two women as sexually insatiable, give them lovers whose bodies are described as animals', and end with their mutilation and execution. The language was probably shocking in Ezekiel's day too.

Two modern positions meet here. One, voiced by Galambush, Weems and others, holds that the text uses a woman's body as a symbol of guilt, with the husband (God) as the only moral agent, and that this has served to excuse abuse. The other, held by Block, Greenberg and Joyce, holds that the metaphor is about a covenant, that it addresses the whole people (men included) as the guilty wife, and that its violence is the violence of war and of ancient law, which the prophet condemns. A reader may hold that both are partly right. The Plain does not soften what the Hebrew says and does not add to it.

The chapter folds three centuries of foreign policy into one story. Samaria's lovers are the Assyrians (Menahem, 2 Kings 15:19–20; Hoshea, 2 Kings 17:3). Jerusalem's are Assyria first (Ahaz, 2 Kings 16:7–9), then Egypt (Hezekiah, Isaiah 30–31; Jehoiakim; Zedekiah, Ezekiel 17:15), and Babylon (Hezekiah's embassy, Isaiah 39; Jehoiakim's early years, 2 Kings 24:1). The pattern repeats: each alliance seems to promise safety, and each turns to disgust (23:17–18, 22, 28). The verb for the disgust, naqa', is used of both the woman and the LORD.

echoes: Ezekiel 16:1–63; Hosea 1:2–3:5; Jeremiah 3:6–11; 2 Kings 15–17; Isaiah 51:17–23; Jeremiah 25:15–29; Jeremiah 7:9–11; John 8:3–11; Revelation 14:10; Revelation 17:1–6

settings.what: The sisters' youth and their lovers
settings.to: The exiles in Babylon, who are told a story about Samaria and Jerusalem
settings.when: No date; most likely the years before the siege (about 591 to 588 BC), after the Temple vision of chapters 8 to 11
settings.why: To show the exiles that Jerusalem's history of alliances is a history of unfaithfulness: Samaria went after Assyria, and Jerusalem, who saw it, went after Assyria, Egypt and Babylon. The purpose is to take away the exiles' belief that the city was a victim.
settings.readers: After 586 the exiles could read the story as an explanation of the fall. Readers in later centuries met the chapter as part of the book's call to repentance.
views: Ezekiel's hearers may have heard the allegory with the same discomfort as modern readers. The text itself notes that people took his speech as mere parables (20:49), so the harshness may be partly an answer to that.
Oholah is Samaria and Oholibah is Jerusalem (23:4). The lovers are the Assyrians, Egyptians and Babylonians; the precise events (Hezekiah's embassy, Zedekiah's treaty) are debated.

settings.what: The lovers turn and the cup
settings.to: Oholibah, the city of Jerusalem, spoken about in front of the exiles; the "you" of 23:22–35
settings.when: No date; before the fall of the city (588 to 586 BC)
settings.why: To tell the exiles that the Babylonians they thought of as friends, the lovers she had turned from, will come against Jerusalem, and that the city will drink her sister's cup.
settings.readers: After 586 the exiles could read the cup of 23:31–34 as the cup they had drunk.

settings.to: The exiles, hearing the charge laid on both Oholah and Oholibah
settings.when: No date; the same period as the rest of the chapter
settings.why: To add the sins that cannot be passed off as politics: child sacrifice and the defiling of the Temple on the same day. It closes with the sentence of the law on adulteresses and the formula "you will know that I am the Lord GOD".
settings.readers: Many critics see 23:36–49 as a later addition because it changes the voice. Later readers took it as the verdict on a long history.

title: The Pot and the Prophet's Wife
sum: On the day the siege of Jerusalem begins, the LORD tells Ezekiel to write down the date, and Ezekiel, who is in Babylon, does (24:1–2). Then he tells a parable of a pot. Meat and bones are cooked in it, but the pot is rusted, and the rust does not come off. At last the empty pot is set on the coals until its bronze glows, so that its uncleanness melts (24:3–14). The pot is the city of bloodshed.

Then comes the saddest passage in the book. The LORD tells Ezekiel that his wife, "the delight of your eyes", will die with a sudden blow, and that he must not mourn (24:15–17). She dies that evening and in the morning he does as he was told (24:18). The people ask what it means, and he tells them that the Temple, their own delight, will be taken and that they too will not be able to mourn (24:19–24). The chapter ends with a promise: a survivor will come, and Ezekiel's mouth will open (24:25–27).
readings: Read as history

Ezekiel's wife died on a real day, and he did not mourn. The date in 24:1 is the actual day the siege began, which he knew in Babylon by the LORD's word. On this reading the chapter records one of the strangest facts of a prophet's life.
Read as sign act

Ezekiel's actions, including the wife's death, are a living parable. The details are less important than the meaning: the exiles will lose Jerusalem and the Temple and will have no way to grieve. Some think the story is told in the way of a parable and not as a biography.
Read through the pot
The two parts of the chapter explain each other. The pot speaks of the city's guilt and punishment. The wife's death shows what it will feel like. Both end on a day that will be "a sign" (24:24, 27).

views.H: The ninth year, tenth month, tenth day (24:1) is the day Nebuchadnezzar began the siege (2 Kings 25:1; Jeremiah 52:4; Jeremiah 39:1 gives the same year and month), about January 588 BC by the count used here. The news of the city's fall came about half a year after the fall in the reckoning of 33:21. The Temple was burned in 586 BC (2 Kings 25:9).
views.C: The two halves of the chapter may come from different times, joined by the theme of 'delight' and 'pot'. The pot song has been seen as a reworking of the proverb of 11:3, and the verses on the pot's emptying (24:9–14) are sometimes seen as a later addition. The date in 24:1 is one of the few in the book that matches a date in 2 Kings, and some critics ask whether it was added after the event.
views.J: The tenth of Tevet (the tenth month, tenth day) became a fast day (compare Zechariah 8:19) that remembers the beginning of the siege. Ezekiel's wife is not named in the text. Later rabbinic law on Leviticus 21:2 counts a priest's wife among the kin he may bury (Bavli Yevamot 22b); that passage does not mention Ezekiel 24:16–17, but it bears on the question of a priest's mourning for his wife.
views.X: Christian readers have seen in the pot a picture of judgment on the city, and in the wife's death a type of the suffering a prophet shares with his people, comparable to Hosea's marriage. Jesus' words about the Temple's coming destruction (Matthew 24:2) can be compared.
views.F: Some futurist readers link the Temple's destruction with later events. Most commentators of every school keep the chapter in 588 to 586 BC.

deep.b: The tenth day of the tenth month is given by Ezekiel (24:1) and by 2 Kings 25:1 and Jeremiah 52:4; Jeremiah 39:1 gives the same year and month but no day. The books count the same year: Jehoiachin's exile began in 597, and Zedekiah's reign began the same year. So the ninth year of the exile is the ninth year of Zedekiah, and the tenth month is Tevet. On the count used here (Judah's royal years numbered from the autumn; Ezekiel's own exile years run from spring, as in the dates at 1:2) the day is January 588 BC and the fall of the city is in July 586, about 30 months later. Some scholars count the years from the spring: the siege still begins in January 588, but the fall is then put in July 587, about 18 months later. The choice between 587 and 586 changes the year of the fall and the length of the siege, not the day of Ezekiel's word; the discussion is in Thiele and in Hayes and Hooker. The date is a rare point where the prophetic book and the history book meet.

Nothing in Ezekiel is more personal than 24:15–18. The Hebrew gives no name, no age and no cause beyond a sudden "blow". The text says only that he spoke in the morning, that she died in the evening and that he obeyed in the morning. Readers have long found the restraint more moving than any detail could be. Most commentators take the event as real and ask what it cost the prophet. The older medical readings, which treated the prophet's silence and signs as symptoms of illness, are a modern tradition with its critics.

The mourning customs he omits are listed in 24:17: weeping aloud, uncovering the head, taking off sandals, covering the upper lip, eating the funeral meal. Each is named as something he does not do. The point is that the exiles will have no rites for the Temple.

deep.h: Poetry and prose in this chapter
deep.b: The pot song (24:3–14) is poetry in lines, and the Plain sets it with slashes. The parts about the date (24:1–2) and the wife (24:15–27) are prose.

echoes: Ezekiel 11:1–13; Ezekiel 33:21–22; 2 Kings 25:1; 2 Kings 25:9; Jeremiah 39:1; Jeremiah 52:4; Jeremiah 16:5–7; Lamentations 2:6–7; Zechariah 8:19

settings.to: The rebellious house, the exiles, to whom Ezekiel tells the parable; the city of Jerusalem is the pot
settings.when: The tenth day of the tenth month of the ninth year, about January 588 BC, the very day Nebuchadnezzar began the siege (2 Kings 25:1)
settings.why: To tell the exiles, who still hoped the city would stand, that the siege had begun that day. The book presents the date as a sign that Ezekiel's word is from the LORD, since he could not have known the day by ordinary means; critical readers ask whether the date was added after the event. The pot answers the leaders' old boast (11:3) that the city was a safe pot for them; now the pot is on the fire.
settings.readers: The exiles who heard the news (33:21) could check Ezekiel's date against the survivor's story. Later readers had the same date from 2 Kings and Jeremiah.

settings.what: The wife's death as a sign
settings.by: The LORD, through Ezekiel's own life
settings.to: The exiles who ask what it means; the speech is to the house of Israel
settings.when: Undated; the evening and morning after the word of 24:15, probably shortly after the siege began
settings.why: The exiles had put their hope in the Temple and the city. Ezekiel's grief he cannot show is the grief they will be unable to show when Jerusalem and the Temple are taken. The sign tells them that the loss will be too great for ordinary rites, and that they will waste away in their guilt.
settings.readers: Exiles after 586 knew that they had not mourned in the usual way, and the passage explained it. Later readers saw the prophet's loss as part of his message.
views: A real death or a sign act
Most commentators take the death as real. A few treat the whole as a literary sign. The Plain follows the text and states no choice.
Shock, fear of the Babylonians, or guilt that makes grief impossible; the text says only that they will waste away in their guilt (24:23).

settings.what: The survivor and the open mouth
settings.to: Ezekiel, with the exiles hearing it
settings.when: Spoken on the day of the sign; fulfilled when the survivor comes, about half a year after the fall (33:21–22)
settings.why: To tell Ezekiel, and through him the exiles, that the silence has an end. The day the survivor comes, the prophet will speak freely, and his silence will have been a sign to them. It closes the first part of the book, judgment on Jerusalem (chapters 1 to 24).
settings.readers: The promise looks forward to chapter 33, where it is kept; readers see the chapters between as written in the waiting.
